title: Evaluating AI-Powered Learning Assistants in Engineering Higher Education: Student Engagement, Ethical Challenges, and Policy Implications
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how students in engineering higher education perceive and use a generative AI learning assistant, with particular attention to trust, ethics, usability, and perceived learning value. The study is motivated by the growing adoption of AI in education and the need to understand not just whether students use such tools, but how concerns about academic integrity, reliability, and institutional policy shape that use. The research is framed around questions comparing AI support with human assistance, identifying barriers to adoption, and examining which academic tasks students find AI most useful for.

The intervention studied is the Educational AI Hub, an AI-powered course-integrated learning assistant that offered several functions: an AI chatbot, notes generation, flashcards, quiz generation and grading, a coding sandbox, and syllabus support. The researchers used an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, combining pre- and post-surveys, system usage logs, and qualitative analysis of student questions submitted to the AI system. The study did not compare the intervention to a control group; instead, it analyzed patterns of use and associations between student perceptions and engagement.

The study took place at a large R1 public university in the Midwest of the United States in two civil and environmental engineering courses, one sophomore-level and one senior-level. Of 77 enrolled students, 65 participated, including mostly Bachelor of Science in Engineering students and 3 Master of Science students; 48 used the AI Hub at least once. Students were introduced to the tool in class and accessed it through the course learning management system. The context was authentic course use across a semester, with engagement concentrated around homework, software support, concept clarification, and assignment-related questions.

The main conclusions are that students viewed the AI assistant as a useful supplement rather than a replacement for instructors or teaching assistants. They rated it especially positively for convenience, comfort, homework help, and concept understanding, but were more mixed about instructional quality and impact on grades. Trust mattered: lower distrust and higher comfort were associated with more use. At the same time, ethical ambiguity and fear of academic misconduct accusations were major barriers, even though most students considered AI use as an academic aid to be ethical and wanted similar tools in other courses. The paper concludes that effective AI integration in higher education requires not only usable, course-aligned tools but also clear faculty guidance and institutional policies to support responsible use.

identified_tools.name: Educational AI Hub
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered learning assistant framework integrated into course learning environments, offering a course-specific chatbot, notes generation, flashcards, quiz generation/grading, coding support, and syllabus question answering for engineering students.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied in two undergraduate civil and environmental engineering courses as a course-integrated AI learning assistant to support homework, concept understanding, studying, software help, and course logistics.

findings.finding_summary: Students perceived the Educational AI Hub as helpful for some learning tasks but not uniformly superior to human support. In post-survey responses, 61% agreed it helped them learn course concepts, 63% agreed it helped them complete homework, 59% reported a positive impact on overall learning, but only 43% agreed it helped them earn a higher grade; instructional quality relative to human support was rated worse by 34%, the same by 49%, and better by 17%.
findings.measure: Post-survey perceived helpfulness for learning concepts, homework completion, overall learning, grades, and comparative quality of help vs. human assistance

findings.finding_summary: Students reported higher comfort and convenience using the AI assistant than traditional human help sources. In the post-survey, 68% rated the tool as more convenient than instructors/TAs/peers, 21% as equally convenient, and 11% as less convenient; 47% felt more comfortable using it, 38% reported no difference, and 15% felt less comfortable. Comfort level with AI was positively associated with system usage (Spearman’s ρ = 0.31, p < 0.05).
findings.measure: Post-survey ratings of convenience and comfort relative to human assistance; correlation between comfort and AI usage

findings.finding_summary: Trust and ethical uncertainty were important barriers to engagement with the Educational AI Hub. In the post-survey, 42% disagreed that they distrusted the AI Hub’s responses, 27% agreed, and 31% were neutral; distrust was negatively associated with usage (Spearman’s ρ = -0.38, p < 0.01). Additionally, 49% agreed they felt apprehensive about using AI in the course, 58% worried about being accused of academic misconduct, and 27% agreed AI use undermines academic integrity while 49% disagreed.
findings.measure: Post-survey distrust, apprehension, academic integrity concerns, misconduct worry, and correlations with AI tool usage

findings.finding_summary: System logs showed strong engagement with the chatbot component of the Educational AI Hub, with 555 chatbot interactions from 46 of 48 active users (96%). Students averaged 13.12 total AI interactions (SD = 11.81), including a mean of 11.56 chatbot messages (SD = 9.437), while structured activity features were used far less often (75 interactions across 15 students; mean total activities = 1.562, SD = 6.687).
findings.measure: System usage logs: interaction counts, feature use frequency, unique users, and descriptive statistics

findings.finding_summary: Students were generally supportive of future AI integration but wanted clearer policy guidance. In survey responses, 83% agreed that using AI as an academic aid is ethical, 80% wanted similar tools in other courses, 59% preferred somewhat restrictive AI policies and 33% preferred even fewer restrictions, while no students supported banning AI outright; however, 42% were uncertain or only somewhat confident about what constitutes academic misconduct when using generative AI.
findings.measure: Post-survey views on ethicality of AI use, future course adoption, policy restrictiveness, and certainty about misconduct boundaries

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with surveys, usage logs, and correlational analyses, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental design and relies heavily on self-reported perceptions. The evidence is useful but limited for causal claims about effectiveness on learning outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive perceptions and engagement patterns, but effects are mostly descriptive percentages and small-to-moderate correlations rather than standardized impacts on academic performance. Direct achievement effects are unclear and mixed, especially for grades.
